title: A hat of twists, drawn fresh
allegory: Variance prompts are like an editor who, before some of a quiz-writer's questions, pulls a random twist card from a hat and clips it to the brief, so a writer copying four pinned examples stops writing the same question three hundred times.
map: the quiz-writer copying four pinned examples
a coin toss before each question, then a random card on heads
append one randomly chosen variance prompt with probability p_var
drawing fresh for every question, never once for the whole run
a pile that spreads across many kinds of question
a wider archetype distribution, so style stops travelling with the property

chapters.name: Three hundred twins
chapters.note: wait, haven't I read this one?

cap.1: You give a model four good test questions and ask for three hundred more. Back come three hundred near-copies: same setting, same shape, same kind of dilemma.
cap.2: Perez et al. (Anthropic, 2022) had a model write 154 eval datasets from instructions and a few examples. ARENA does the same from four examples, and unvaried few-shot generation gives no real coverage.
cap.3: Few-shot prompting narrows the generator hard around the exemplars' archetypes, so independent calls return near-duplicates. You need a deliberate diversity lever, resampled per call.

cap.1: A quiz-writer copies four pinned examples. Before some questions, an editor pulls a random card from a hat, like 'make it simple', and clips it to the brief.
cap.2: Variance prompts are a short list of extra instructions, such as 'break the pattern', 'introduce unusual contexts', 'make these really simple'. With probability p_var, one is picked at random and appended to that call.
cap.3: The hat holds instructions like 'identify what makes these repetitive and break the pattern'. Per call, with probability p_var, append one chosen at random. It widens the archetype distribution; it is not there to raise average quality.

chapters.name: Built fresh per call
chapters.title: five calls, each prompt built from scratch (p_var = 0.5)

cap.1: Each question gets its own prompt, built from scratch: the four examples in a new order, a coin toss, and on heads, a card from the hat.
cap.2: Per API call: resample the few-shot examples so their order changes, then with probability p_var append a randomly chosen variance prompt. Structured output keeps every variant parseable JSON.
cap.3: Each item is an independent draw from a mixture of prompts: the plain one with weight 1 − p_var, each of K twisted ones with weight p_var / K. A Pydantic response_format holds every draw to the schema.

chapters.name: Same card, new rut

right.title: a fresh draw per question
lines: coin and card inside the loop
each call gets its own twist

chapters.verdict: The randomness has to live inside the loop.

cap.1: The classic slip: pick one twist card at the start and clip it to every brief. Now you have three hundred 'really simple' questions. A new rut, same problem.
cap.2: Appending the same variance prompt to every call defeats the entire purpose. Sample it inside the per-question function, so each call can get a different one, or none.
cap.3: One variance prompt chosen per run is a constant shift of the conditional, not added diversity. Resample per item, and read twenty outputs yourself before generating three hundred.

cap.1: If every question is written the same way, the thing you test and the style always arrive together. When the model reacts, which one did it react to?
cap.2: Variance prompts aren't there to raise average quality. They widen the spread of question archetypes so style stops travelling with the property, and your score measures the property.
cap.3: Uniform style makes style a confounder of the behaviour you score. A related leak: when one model writes the answer and the distractors, option length can predict answer_matching_behavior. Measure it; shuffle options.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Style must not predict the score
Read twenty before making three hundred

cap.1: Evals are how we check what AI systems really do. Hundreds of questions only count if they differ; otherwise the score measures your writing style.
cap.2: Perez et al.'s scale let them see bigger, more RLHF-trained models getting more sycophantic, a trend you can't see on forty questions. Variety is what makes scale count.
cap.3: Generation makes questions cheap; quality control makes them mean something. Diverse archetypes plus balance checks keep an eval measuring the behaviour you want to understand and steer.

coda.title: Shake the hat: how many kinds of question come out? (toy)

params.label: p_var: chance a question gets a twist
bug: draw one card for the whole run (0 = fresh, 1 = once)

coda.f: once ? [0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0] : [1 - p].concat(range(5).map(i => i < K ? p / K : 0))

readouts.label: share for each twist card
readouts.f: once ? 'card 1 gets all of them' : round(100*p/K) + '% each'

caption.1: Slide p_var and the number of cards, then flip the bug switch. The effective number of question styles only grows when every question gets a fresh draw.
caption.2: Toy model: each card pushes a question into its own style. Fresh draws spread the pile over up to K + 1 styles; one card clipped to every call gives one style, no better than no twists.
caption.3: Effective styles = exp(entropy) of the shares: 1 − p plain, p/K per card. It peaks at K + 1 when p = K/(K + 1). Real cards overlap and quality varies, so read the spread, not the peak.

where_else: Synthetic training data and data augmentation: deliberate random perturbation so a model can't lean on one incidental style
Sampling temperature: randomness at the level of tokens rather than instructions
Quality control in [3.2]: generation makes questions cheap, quality control makes them mean something

hamming.what: Extra instructions, drawn at random per call and appended with probability p_var, that push a few-shot generator away from repeating one archetype.
hamming.when: Whenever you generate a dataset from a handful of examples, as with ARENA [3.2]'s eval questions, and the outputs start to look alike.
hamming.why: Few-shot examples make outputs consistent, so without deliberate variety the dataset loses coverage and question style gets tangled up with the property you measure.

object.title: The question sorter
object.subtitle: Twelve generated questions, one per row, each dropped into a style column: plain, or pushed by one of five twist cards.

knobs.label: Bug: one card for the whole run

cap.1: Twelve generated questions, one per row. Columns are styles: plain, or pushed by twist card 1 to 5. With no twists, all twelve land in the plain column.
cap.2: p_var = 0: pure few-shot generation. Every question comes from the same prompt, so every one has the same archetype.
cap.3: With p_var = 0 every item is drawn from one conditional; the style distribution is a point mass.

cap.1: Turn p_var up to one half. Half the questions draw a card and the hat picks which one, so the pile spreads over four columns.
cap.2: p_var = 0.5 with three cards: each call tosses its own coin and, on heads, picks its own card. Here 6 of 12 stay plain; the rest split 1, 3 and 2 across the cards.
cap.3: Per-item resampling makes the style label an independent draw per row: plain with probability 1 − p_var, each card with p_var / K.

cap.1: Now the bug: one card drawn for the whole run and clipped to every call. All twelve questions move, together, into one new column.
cap.2: Choosing the variance prompt outside the loop: every question gets the same twist, so the dataset is exactly as uniform as before, in a new style.
cap.3: A per-run draw is a constant shift of the conditional: the style distribution is still a point mass, just somewhere else.

cap.1: A bigger hat and a higher p_var spread the questions wider: every column gets used. Twelve can't fill six styles evenly, which is one reason you make hundreds.
cap.2: Five cards at p_var = 0.8: 3 questions stay plain, the other 9 scatter over all five cards. Small samples are lumpy, so judge spread on the full set.
cap.3: Expected shares are 1 − p_var and p_var / K, but a 12-item sample is noisy; coverage claims need the full generated set.

cap.1: p_var at 1: every question gets a twist and the plain column empties. None stay close to your four examples. The dial sets the mix.
cap.2: At p_var = 1 no question comes from the plain few-shot prompt; the mix is entirely twisted archetypes.
cap.3: p_var sets the mixture weight on the unperturbed conditional; at 1 it drops to zero.

predict.q: You pick one variance prompt at the start and append it to every call. What happens to diversity?

options.t: Nothing gained: every question shifts into the same new rut
It rises, since every question now has a twist

predict.why: Diversity comes from drawing fresh per question. One card on every call just moves the whole pile together.

options.t: Widening the spread of question styles, so style doesn't track the property
Raising the average quality of each question

predict.why: They widen the archetype distribution; average quality is the job of good examples and quality control.

predict.q: A model scores 90% on an MCQ set it wrote itself. What do you check first?

options.t: Whether option length or letter position predicts the label
Whether the model is just very capable

predict.why: The same model wrote answer and distractors, so the matching option is often the long, careful one. You may have built a length detector.

object.where: Anywhere a generator is pinned by examples: synthetic data, test generation, data augmentation.
